newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU looks for any Creditanstalt subsidy.
newsitem.headline: EU looks for any Creditanstalt subsidy.

text.p: The European Commission is probing whether the sale of Austria's second-largest bank Creditanstalt to the country's market leader Bank Austria involves any public subsidies, a Commission spokesman said on Monday.

The probe into the 17.2 billion schilling ($1.5 billion) deal, which was prompted by unspecified "remarks and complaints", also focused on the guarantee attached by the City of Vienna to Bank Austria's present and future liabilities.

Bank Austria, which is controlled by the City of Vienna, won a bid on Sunday for the state's 70-percent stake in Creditanstalt-Bankverein after a bitter battle which divided the the Social Democrat-conservative government coalition.

The spokesman's comments came as no surprise. In December, the Austrian Finance Ministry confirmed press reports that the EU's competition watchdog was seeking information on the privatisation of Creditanstalt and particularly Bank Austria's bid.
The Commission must vet whether the sale has involved any direct or disguised subsidies.
The municipal guarantee given to Bank Austria could effectively amount to state aid as it enables it to have a triple-A rating and compete with commercial banks for cheaper credit.
The privatisation of Creditanstalt is also expected to be examined under the European Union's merger rules which ban creation or strengthening of dominant positions, the spokesman said.

Belgian Bacob bank, a member of the consortium led by insurer EA-Generali which also put in a bid for Creditanstalt, said on Friday that the sale to Bank Austria would raise anti-trust issues for the Austrian banking industry.
Bacob spokesman Guido Mertens told Reuters the new bank would become six times bigger than its closest competitor.
Creditanstalt's sale is expected to be followed by a flurry of takeovers in the country's traditionally overcrowded financial scene.

Experts said it would force other Austrian banks to seek out partners in order to shore up their market position or risk being swept away by a tide of increased competition at the start of a single European currency.

With total assets of some 1,400 billion schillings, the combined bank will control 80 percent of Vienna bourse trading, half of the Austria's export financing and 70 percent of the country's commercial banking.
Bank Austria agreed to be taken out of public control successively and to see the City of Vienna's influence of the bank reduced. ($ = 11.14 Austrian Schillings)
